```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

load in required libraries
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggalluvial)
library(tidyverse)
```

we read in the data we received below
```{r}
chem205 = read.csv("chem205master2024.csv", header = TRUE)
```

After getting a glimpse of the data, I seek to clean it to remove NAs and make it easier to work with. i do that below
```{r}
#NAs are removed here and replaced with 0s. Since these features acted binary, this just makes analysis easier
chem205 = chem205 %>%
  mutate(across(c(StudyGroupsYN.Registered.Sep9, StudyGroupsYN.Waitlisted.Sep9, TutoringYN.Sep9, Workshop_1.Sun, Workshop_1.Mon, Workshop_3.Sun, Workshop_3.Mon), ~ ifelse(is.na(.), 0, 1)))

#We make sure the features that are supposed to purely numeric are like so. This code turns any entries that werent numbers into NAs
chem205 = chem205 %>%
mutate(Exam2.Score_raw = as.numeric(Exam2.Score_raw),
       Exam3.Score_raw = as.numeric(Exam3.Score_raw),
       ExamFinal.Score_raw = as.numeric(ExamFinal.Score_raw),
       Homework.Achieve = as.numeric(Homework.Achieve))

#Unnecessary code here
#chem205$Exam2.Score_raw[is.na(chem205$Exam2.Score_raw)] = 0
#chem205$Exam3.Score_raw[is.na(chem205$Exam3.Score_raw)] = 0
#chem205$ExamFinal.Score_raw[is.na(chem205$ExamFinal.Score_raw)] = 0
#chem205$Homework.Achieve[is.na(chem205$Homework.Achieve)] = 0
```
I subset the data below for students who withdrew. will look into this in the file
```{r}
withdraw = chem205[chem205$Grade.FINAL == "W", ]
```

our first task is to get familiar with the data and the variables present, pick out the most important variables, and start to ask questions. We look at levels of variables below

```{r}
table(chem205$Student.Classification)
```

While mostly freshmen, the counts of juniors and sophomores shouldn't be wrote off. I compare their quantitative assessments below

```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Student.Classification) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Quantitative.Score),
            median_score = median(Quantitative.Score),
            sd_score = sd(Quantitative.Score))
```
as the medians are larger than the means, it is likely each group has some low outliers, especially juniors. Sophomores look to be much better off than the other groups.


```{r}
table(chem205$Instructor.code)
```

Prof W and Z look to have much less students than prof V and Z. Lets see the profs' average final grades to see if this affected students

```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Instructor.code) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Grade.Final..),
            median_score = median(Grade.Final..),
            sd_score = sd(Grade.Final..))
```
Class size may have played a minor role; prof Z had the smallest class and the highest average grade, and prof Y had one of the largest and had the lowest average grade. However, with such a small sample size, it is difficult to conclude anything about class size. The only thing I can conclude with reasonable confidence is that prof Z must have been a pretty good prof

below we check average final grades for the class years
```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Student.Classification) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Grade.Final..),
            median_score = median(Grade.Final..),
            sd_score = sd(Grade.Final..))
```
similar relationship to quant assessment. sophomores look good (scores are about symmetric too) and juniors look the worst


For exam 1, I want to see how engagement is correlated with scores. we look at tables below
```{r}
table(chem205$Engagement.Exam1.tot.max4.)
```
Not surprised that not many students engaged a ton. we will see how this affects exam scores

```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Engagement.Exam1.tot.max4.) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Exam1.Score_raw),
            median_score = median(Exam1.Score_raw),
            sd_score = sd(Exam1.Score_raw))
```

interesting relationship: those that got the most help did the best on average (3) but the step below (2) ended up doing the worst of all groups. what separates 2 and 3? I look at exam 2 results below to see if it holds

no variable exists measuring the amount of engagement in the span of exam 1 to exam 2 and making it isnt exaclty possible due to lack of info except for workshop attendance. going forward, will measure with overall engagement sum. will analyze exam 1 scores with this in mind
```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Engagmenet.sum) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Exam1.Score_raw),
            median_score = median(Exam1.Score_raw),
            sd_score = sd(Exam1.Score_raw))
```
another interesting relationship in that the middle looks to be the lowest, and 0 and 8 are some of the highest with 0 having the lowest variance. we look at exam 2 and 3 below

```{r}
chem205 = chem205 %>%
  mutate(Exam2.Score_raw = as.numeric(Exam2.Score_raw))
```

```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Engagmenet.sum) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Exam2.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_score = median(Exam2.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_score = sd(Exam2.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE))
```
Scores were pretty varied across groups. however the variance for the 8 group is the lowest

```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Engagmenet.sum) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Exam3.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_score = median(Exam3.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_score = sd(Exam3.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE))
```
weirdly enough, those with 0 engagement seemed to have the most consistently high exam grades. High engagement is kind of inconsistent, but has consistently low variance on what grade they obtain now i want to see final grades

```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Engagmenet.sum) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Grade.Final.., na.rm = TRUE),
            median_score = median(Grade.Final.., na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_score = sd(Grade.Final.., na.rm = TRUE))
```
We have seen that the groups with the highest grades are those with 0 or 7/8 engagement; two opposite ends of the spectrum. However, i do think this is because those who already are confident with the content (0) are on par with those who used the most out of their resources (7/8). However those in the middle seem to have done the worst, which feels backwards

to verify my above statement, i compare the quant assessment with engagement levels
```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Engagmenet.sum) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Quantitative.Score, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_score = median(Quantitative.Score, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_score = sd(Quantitative.Score, na.rm = TRUE))
```
It seems I was about right; those with 0 engagement seem to already be confident in the content and were adequately prepared, whereas other groups were less so. Interestingly, those with 1 engagement scored high on the quant assessment but proved to be the group that performed the worst in the class

Thus, for the question, "does engagement correlate with success in the course?", i would be unsure, since the only groups that had consistently high success were 0 and 7/8, with every other group being all over the place. However, this is at a very general lens; i did not analyze for specific practices (tlc, office hours, etc.) so they can have different relationships with grades

we now look at other variables. I want to see if homework grades are linked to final grade achieved in the course


```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(Grade.Final.Binned) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Homework.Achieve, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_score = median(Homework.Achieve, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_score = sd(Homework.Achieve, na.rm = TRUE))
```
Yes? F's and W's have a significantly lower grade compared to all the others, which makes sense. All the other grades are only a few points apart but are all in the 90's. So none of the passing grades had a necessarily "bad" homework grade


Now, I want to run multiple linear regression on multiple variables on overall engagement, the quantitative assessment, and then both. To do this, we need to analyze the levels in the engagement columns and then change the entries to be quantitative.

```{r}
table(chem205$split_engagement_workshop)
table(chem205$split_engagement_faculty)
table(chem205$split_engagement_tutoring)
table(chem205$split_engagement_studygroups)
```
We observe these variables are binary. Thus, we change them to be either 0 or 1, with 1 denoting the positive outcome for engagement, and 0 the option which had little engagement

```{r}
chem205$split_engagement_workshop = ifelse(chem205$split_engagement_workshop == "1 or more", 1, 0)
chem205$split_engagement_faculty = ifelse(chem205$split_engagement_faculty == "frequent", 1, 0)
chem205$split_engagement_studygroups = ifelse(chem205$split_engagement_studygroups == "sustained", 1, 0)
chem205$split_engagement_tutoring = ifelse(chem205$split_engagement_tutoring == "1 or more", 1, 0)
```

as the variables are now numeric, we can proceed with regression. We create 3 initial models: a model including the variables above, a model with only the quantitative assessment score, and both combined. we do the first model below

```{r}
model1 = lm(Grade.Final.. ~ split_engagement_workshop + split_engagement_faculty + split_engagement_studygroups + split_engagement_tutoring, data = chem205)
summary(model1)
```
```{r}
model2 = lm(Grade.Final.. ~ Quantitative.Score, data = chem205)
summary(model2)
```

```{r}
model3 = lm(Grade.Final.. ~ split_engagement_workshop + split_engagement_faculty + split_engagement_studygroups + split_engagement_tutoring + Quantitative.Score, data = chem205)
summary(model3)
```
We see model 2 is statistically significant, which makes sense. However, model 1 did a lot worse than I thought. model 3 is also iffy. we see engagement with faculty became significant in model 3. we see what happens in a model with just the quant assessment score and faculty engagement below. We also apply a transformation on y to see if it better fits the data

```{r}
model4 = lm(Grade.Final..^2 ~ split_engagement_faculty +  Quantitative.Score, data = chem205)
summary(model4)
```
This is the best trivial model I can make. While the R^2 isn't flattering (0.38 is moderate in strength) all variables are now significant. faculty dos also meaningfully add to the model, justifying its addition to the model. However, it is likely that other engagement variables may also end up being useful in future models.

```{r}

  summarise(n = n(),
            exam1 = mean(Exam1.Score_raw),
            sd1_score = sd(Exam1.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            exam2 = mean(Exam2.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),

            exam3 = mean(Exam3.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd3_score = sd(Exam3.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),

            sdfin_score = sd(ExamFinal.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE))
```
surprisingly, the 0-3 group just barely beats out the 4-8 group in exam scores. however, the values are so close together that i wouldnt consider the difference meaningful, even if the variances for the 0-3 group are higher

we check the quantitiative assessment score below
```{r}
chem205 %>%
  group_by(split_engagement_total) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Quantitative.Score),
            median_score = median(Quantitative.Score),
            sd_score = sd(Quantitative.Score, na.rm = TRUE))
```
not surprisingly, the group with less engagement has a slight edge over the group that has more engagement. i am inclined to believe that higher quantitative assessment score leads to less engagement. we have actually seen this: the 1st quartile seems to have the least amount of engagement on average

I am curious in what class years make up each group. we observe this below
```{r}
chem205 %>%
  count(Student.Classification, split_engagement_total)
```
most of those that engaged a lot with resources with freshmen. this makes sense, since they are more eager to utilize resources

for the engagement groups, we also look at how many students were DFW
```{r}
chem205 %>%
  count(DFW.Counter, split_engagement_total)
```
almost 1/4 of those that didnt engage much were DFW. i feel like this makes sense, since 0-3 is comprised of those who struggled but also those who succeeded the most

related to this, i want to compare course grades / exam scores for those who were not DFW for both groups

```{r}
chem205[chem205$DFW.Counter == 0, ] %>%
  group_by(split_engagement_total) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            exam1 = mean(Exam1.Score_raw),
            sd1_score = sd(Exam1.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            exam2 = mean(Exam2.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd2_score = sd(Exam2.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            exam3 = mean(Exam3.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd3_score = sd(Exam3.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            finalexam = mean(ExamFinal.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE),
            sdfin_score = sd(ExamFinal.Score_raw, na.rm = TRUE))
```
obv exam scores are higher, but there is a bigger difference between exam scores between groups which is not surprising and variances are about the same

related to the above, no we look at the final course grades
```{r}
chem205[chem205$DFW.Counter == 0, ] %>%
  group_by(split_engagement_total) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_score = mean(Grade.Final..),
            median_score = median(Grade.Final..),
            sd_score = sd(Grade.Final.., na.rm = TRUE))
```
like above there is now a distinct difference for both groups in 0-3's favor (they got B - B+s on average)

sum(chem205$Workshop_1.Sun)
sum(chem205$Workshop_1.Mon)
sum(chem205$Workshop_2.Sun)
sum(chem205$Workshop_2.Mon)
